title: Soft-start heating probe — field log
content:
Purpose:
Quick, messy scratchpad for the soft-start / heating probe experiment. Trying to capture what I ran, what I saw, and the immediate hypotheses. This is not a polished report — notes to self / for Theo + Isha sync.

Context / motivation:
- We keep seeing p99 spikes during rapid QPS ramps (esp when servers go from cold -> steady). Hypothesis: aggressive batching + sudden influx causes queueing + long-tail kernel wakeups and poor KV-cache priming.
- Idea: 'soft-start' ingress shaping — ramp traffic up in micro-steps (100ms windows) for first N seconds to allow GPU kernels and KV cache to warm without blocking high-priority requests. Want to quantify whether this reduces p99 by reducing tail outliers and how it affects sustained throughput / mean latency.

Experiment summary (single-run log):
- Host: local dev cluster (2x A100-simulated nodes via perf harness)
- Model: llama-like-13B-8bit (quantized test build q8bhv)
- Harness: bench-runner v0.6.1 (custom arrival pattern script)
- Arrival pattern: sudden spike from 10 qps baseline to 800 qps sustained for 90s, preceded by two variants: (A) immediate ramp (control), (B) soft-start ramp (100ms micro-steps, 8 steps to reach full target over 800ms).
- Requests: 64-token completions, top-p sampling disabled, deterministic-ish (random prefixes from sample corpus).
- KV cache state: cold at t0 (no priming), separate run with primed cache (10 warm requests) done later.

Commands used (approx):
- control: bench-runner --pattern spike --start-qps 10 --target-qps 800 --duration 90 --model q8bhv
- soft-start: bench-runner --pattern soft-start --start-qps 10 --target-qps 800 --steps 8 --step-interval-ms 100 --duration 90 --model q8bhv

Observed metrics (single run outputs, trimmed):
- Control (immediate ramp):
  - achieved throughput plateau: 780 qps
  - p50: 18 ms, p95: 132 ms, p99: 628 ms
  - error rate (server 5xx): 0.3% (sporadic timeouts at minute 0:10–0:15)
  - gpu_util (avg across nodes): 89% after 6s, spikes to 99% for short windows then some kernel-level stalls visible in perf traces
  - KV cache hit after start: ~4% in first 15s, rising slowly to 48% by 60s

- Soft-start (8x steps @100ms):
  - achieved throughput plateau: 770 qps (slightly lower, within noise)
  - p50: 19 ms, p95: 98 ms, p99: 226 ms
  - error rate: 0.04% (one timeout)
  - gpu_util: ramps smoother; 75% at 1s, 86% at 3s, 92% steady; fewer short 99% spikes
  - KV cache hit after start: ~18% in first 15s, 62% by 60s

Quick ASCII-ish time slices (tail snapshots):
- Control p99 trace (seconds): [120ms, 140ms, 210ms, 680ms, 320ms, 540ms, 610ms, 290ms, (2x 900ms outliers at 12s, 14s)]
- Soft-start p99 trace: [110ms, 120ms, 130ms, 150ms, 170ms, 200ms, 210ms, 230ms]

Initial interpretation / why this matters:
- Soft-start visibly reduced p99 by ~60% in this test — outliers reduced and the extreme long tails nearly eliminated. Suggests that many long tails were caused by sudden kernel wakeups + cache cold misses that cascade into larger queues.
- KV cache primed faster under soft-start: higher early hit-rate. Likely because micro-steps produced small groups of similar prefixes that warmed KV entries before larger batches formed.
- Slight reduction in achieved throughput (780 -> 770 qps) is within noise; no evidence of steady-state throughput regression.
- Error rate reduced significantly; likely fewer transient timeouts when load arrives gently.

Caveats / things to validate next:
- This is a single run on a simulated dev cluster (not full prod fleet). Need to repeat across different models (7B / 70B), different hardware (multi-gpu, heterogeneous), and with real client mix (varied token lengths, embeddings).
- Investigate whether batch formation logic in runtime interacts with soft-start parameters — e.g., if step interval too long we may break batching efficiency. Run a sweep: steps = [4,8,16], interval-ms = [50,100,200].
- Trace-level analysis: collect kernel timestamps and queue times to confirm that the source of p99 reduction is kernel wakeups vs long queue accumulation.
- Check impact on latency-sensitive priority lanes — does soft-start delay high-priority small requests if applied globally? Consider applying soft-start only to new model-allocations or low-priority queues.

Immediate next steps (actionable):
1) Re-run a 5-trial suite on the same config and capture median p99 and variance.
2) Run a short sweep for step counts / intervals to find knee (balance warmup vs batch efficiency).
3) Run one test with cache-primed baseline to isolate cache effect from kernel wakeups.
4) Add perf traces (nvprof/simpler kernel timestamps) for one run to correlate stalls.
5) Sync with runtime team (Theo) to discuss feasibility of introducing an ingress soft-start policy at router/orchestrator-layer.

Notes to self:
- If we implement soft-start in the router, make it configurable per-deployment and per-model-version (some versions may prefer immediate ramp for bursty real-time workloads).
- Consider hybrid: apply micro soft-start for first 1500 requests or 5s, then hand off to normal shaping.

Loose mental model:
- sudden spike -> huge batch formation + many cold KV misses -> first batches are expensive and block subsequent requests -> queue grows -> tail explodes.
- soft-start -> small groups warm kernels/KV -> subsequent large batches are more efficient -> queue doesn't blow out.

Relevant artifacts and quick links: PR for bench-runner pattern: https://github.com/redwood-inference/bench-runner/pull/56
Perf trace notes (placeholder): https://drive.internal/redwood/perf-traces/soft-start-2024-11-04.tgz

End quick log. Will run repeats tomorrow and record clean CSVs in the shared perf bucket.

-- Marisol
(added 2024-11-07 quick numbers after one re-run)
